rows.name: multipart-pause-1500
rows.question: For exactly ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block, compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element. Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounds check. Explain the arithmetic.
rows.recognizedQuestion: For example, ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounce check Explain the arithmetic
rows.answer: You need 53 blocks. Since 52 × 192 = 9,984, the final block has 10,000 − 9,984 = 16 active threads. In total, 53 × 192 = 10,176 threads launch, so 176 are out of range. Interpreting “bounce check” as “bounds check,” all launched threads should test index < 10,000; those 176 fail the check and skip processing.

rows.name: switch-topic
rows.question: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.answer:
Atomicity makes each transaction all-or-nothing; it doesn’t make concurrent transactions behave as if they ran serially. Under snapshot isolation, both transactions can read the same old state, pass their checks, and update different rows without a write conflict.

For example, two doctors are on call, and at least one must remain. Each transaction sees both on call and takes its own doctor off call. Because they update different rows, both can commit, leaving nobody on call—write skew. Serializable isolation, or properly coordinated locking around the shared invariant, prevents this.

review.note: Correct atomicity versus serializability distinction,disjoint-row conflict limitation,two-doctor counterexample and serializable/coordinated-lock remedy.
review.usefulPrefix: Atomicity makes each transaction all-or-nothing; it doesn’t make concurrent transactions behave as if they ran serially.
